segments.title: Introduction to Big O Notation in Computer Science

sub_topics.name: Introduction
sub_topics.description: Hey, what's going on everybody? It's your bro, hope you're doing well, and in this video I'm going to describe the very basics of Big O notation in, well, computer science.

sub_topics.name: What is Big O Notation
sub_topics.description: So sit back, relax, and enjoy the show. Oh yeah, Big O notation. So a common phrase used with Big O notation is, how code slows as data grows. It describes the performance of an algorithm as the amount of data increases.

key_points: Big O notation is used to describe the performance of an algorithm
It describes how code slows as data grows

segments.title: Understanding Big O Notation with Examples

sub_topics.name: Example 1: Addup Function
sub_topics.description: Here's a more concrete example. I have a function named addup. We will add up to a certain number depending on what we pass in as an argument. The for loop within here will iterate once up to whatever number that n is, add i to sum, then return it.

sub_topics.name: Example 2: Optimized Addup Function
sub_topics.description: Now another way which we could write the same function is to take sum equals n times n plus 1 divided by 2. We will get the exact same sum. So if n was, let's say, a million, this is still only going to take a couple seconds.

key_points: Big O notation can be used to analyze the performance of different algorithms
Optimized algorithms can significantly improve performance
Big O notation helps compare the performance of different algorithms

segments.title: Understanding Different Runtime Complexities

sub_topics.name: Constant Time
sub_topics.description: Here's a graph that I made to represent the different runtime complexities. We have data on the x-axis represented by n. So data will increase as we go more to the right, and we have time on the y-axis.

sub_topics.name: Logarithmic Time and Linear Time
sub_topics.description: Anything that has a runtime complexity of O of 1 will take the same amount of time regardless of the data size. A few examples would include the random access of an element within an array and inserting at the beginning of a linked list.

sub_topics.name: Quasi-Linear Time, Quadratic Time, and Factorial Time
sub_topics.description: Next we have O of N log N, also known as quasi-linear time. This would include a quick sort, merge sort, and heap sort. We'll talk about these concepts in future videos.

key_points: Constant time has a fixed performance regardless of data size
Logarithmic time and linear time have different performance characteristics
Quadratic time and factorial time can be very slow for large data sets
